title: The Four Great Kingdoms as the Ordered Fullness of Natural Dominion
arc: The teaching surveys the four great kingdoms of the world as a complete fourfold ordering of natural rule, naming them in sequence up to the fourth (the kingship of Sileus), and concludes that none stands exalted exceedingly above the others — so that natural dominion is distributed in ordered fullness without any single earthly seat reaching above its own state.
reading:
Although the surface of this teaching is geographic and political — a list of four ruling kingdoms that stand in the world — its correspondential force lies in the number and the comparison. Four is the number of ordered fullness in extension: the cosmic order articulated in all directions, the four climes through which the natural is completely measured. When the master numbers the great kingdoms of the world as four, and walks through them up to the fourth (named here the kingship of Sileus, with the third and the others now lost behind the lacunae), he is not merely cataloguing nations. He is showing the natural plane of dominion as a complete fourfold structure — the full extension of rule as it can be borne in ultimates.

The kingdom (ⲙⲛⲧⲣ̄ⲡⲟ) at this register signifies a state of governance in the natural mind: a confirmed dominion of one ruling principle over a region of life. To say there are four such kingdoms in the cosmos is to say that the natural-rational interface, in its dimension of authority, is articulated in four discrete states. Each holds its own clime; each rules within its own boundary; none is the celestial throne. The kingdoms here belong to the cosmos — the mingled state — not to the aeon. They are the dignities of the natural, the highest reach of rule that the world as world can produce.

The closing observation is the spiritual key: of these four great kingdoms, "there is none exalted exceedingly above them." Read correspondentially, this is not a remark of equivalence among empires but a doctrine about the ceiling of natural dominion. Within the cosmos, no earthly kingship rises beyond the fourfold horizon of natural rule. Each is great only within its own state. The implication, by negation, is that whatever is exalted exceedingly above them must belong to another order altogether — to the King of Honor's judicial dominion over the firmaments, and beyond that to the Father of Greatness whose Greatness has no measure. The four kingdoms thus stand in the teaching as the full natural ordering of dignity, set as a floor against which the heavenly kingship is silently distinguished.

Because the central names of the first and second kingdoms have fallen into the gaps (only the third register and the fourth — Sileus — survive intact), the specific correspondence of each individual kingdom cannot be recovered from the surface of this fragment. What remains intact is the doctrine of fourfoldness and the doctrine of the ceiling: that natural rule, however great, is enclosed within its four-cornered extension, and that the inmost authority is not to be sought among the kingdoms of the world.
